edits.why_correct: Failure of eyelid closure in a lower motor neurone facial palsy exposes the cornea, which can dry out, ulcerate and scar. Eye care is therefore part of initial management: regular lubricating drops during the day, and ointment with gentle taping of the lid at night. Pain, redness or visual change should prompt same-day ophthalmology review. Source: RCEM Learning, Acute facial palsy management; consistent with NICE CKS, Bell's palsy.

edits.why_correct: Long-standing chronic ear disease can spread to the adjacent temporal lobe or cerebellum, forming an abscess. The combination of headache, fever, vomiting, drowsiness and a focal cerebellar sign points to a space-occupying intracranial infection, which needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical and microbiology input. Source: standard teaching on intracranial complications of chronic suppurative otitis media (see NICE CKS, Otitis media - chronic suppurative).

edits.why_correct: A positive Romberg test, where balance worsens when vision is removed, indicates loss of proprioceptive (or vestibular) input, because the eyes normally compensate for the missing sensory information. With reduced vibration and joint position sense in a diabetic patient, the picture fits a sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy. Source: standard clinical neurology examination teaching (Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine).

Clinically fine, but NG217 does not define ictal phases (writer's own note), so the citation is misleading.

edits.why_correct: The postictal phase is the recovery period after a seizure, in which drowsiness, confusion, headache and sometimes transient focal weakness are common. It follows the ictal phase (the seizure itself) and gradually resolves. Source: standard epilepsy terminology (ILAE seizure classification).

CKS meralgia paraesthetica could not be verified (CKS 403; searches found no CKS/NHS page), so 'verified against CKS' is unsupported. Clinical content (LFCN entrapment, obesity/belts, conservative management) is standard and supported by Cochrane/reviews. Citation replaced; management wording softened. No live meralgia item.

edits.why_correct: Isolated burning and numbness over the anterolateral thigh with normal power and reflexes is typical of meralgia paraesthetica, entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, a purely sensory nerve. Obesity, weight gain, pregnancy and tight belts or clothing are recognised triggers. Management is conservative: reassurance, removing the trigger and weight loss, with neuropathic pain treatment or specialist referral if symptoms persist. Source: Cochrane Review, Treatment for meralgia paraesthetica; standard clinical neurology teaching.
